title: Web Cache Deception: How A GraphQL Query in the Archives Led Me to Cached Profile Data
summary_en: A GraphQL endpoint was found to accept GET requests and ignore trailing file extensions, allowing an attacker to trick a cache into storing sensitive user profile data as a public static file.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability stems from a mismatch between how the application server and the caching layer (a middleman server that stores copies of files) interpret URLs. The application server was configured to ignore trailing file extensions like '.pdf' and process the underlying GraphQL route, while the cache saw the extension and assumed the response was a non-sensitive static file. Furthermore, the server allowed sensitive operations via GET requests (parameters in the URL) instead of strictly requiring POST requests (parameters in the hidden body), making the request eligible for caching.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher searched web archives for historical requests to find hidden functionality.
GET /api/query/publicContent?query=...&variables=...
Why: To see if the server accepts GraphQL queries via GET requests (parameters in the URL) instead of just POST (parameters in the hidden body).

DISCOVERY
2. The researcher logged into a test account and identified the standard request for profile data.
POST /api/query/accountProfile
Why: To find an endpoint (a specific web address) that handles sensitive personal information.
3. The researcher converted the authenticated POST request into a GET request.
GET /api/query/accountProfile?query={accountProfile...}&variables=...
Why: GET requests are frequently cached by internet infrastructure, whereas POST requests are typically ignored by caches.

EXPLOITATION
4. The researcher appended a fake file extension to the end of the URL path.
https://example.com/api/query/accountProfile.pdf?query=...
Why: To perform Web Cache Deception (tricking a cache into storing dynamic data as a static file). The '.pdf' suffix tells the cache this is a public document.
5. The researcher sent this modified request while logged in with a session cookie (a digital ID card used for authentication).
Cookie: session=REDACTED
Why: To force the server to generate a response containing private data that the cache will then save.
6. The researcher checked the HTTP headers (extra info sent with a request) for a cache 'HIT'.
X-Cache: HIT
Why: A 'HIT' means the cache has stored a copy of the response and will serve it to the next person who asks.

IMPACT
7. The researcher opened a private browser window with no cookies and requested the exact same URL.
https://example.com/api/query/accountProfile.pdf?query=...
Why: To verify if an unauthenticated stranger can see the cached private data of the first user.
8. The researcher successfully retrieved the cached JSON (a data format) containing the test account's address and phone number.
Why: The cache served the stored 'PDF' (which was actually private JSON) to the unauthorized requester.
lesson.example: Imagine a site 'target.example' that shows your private inbox at '/api/v1/messages'. The server is programmed to ignore anything after the slash, so '/api/v1/messages/anything' still shows your messages. An attacker crafts a link: 'https://target.example/api/v1/messages/style.css'. When a logged-in victim clicks this, the server returns their private messages. However, the CDN (Content Delivery Network, a type of cache) sees the '.css' extension and thinks, 'This is just a public stylesheet, I will save a copy.' The attacker then visits 'https://target.example/api/v1/messages/style.css' themselves and the CDN gives them the victim's private messages from its memory.
lesson.takeaway: Always test if sensitive POST endpoints also work as GET requests, as this is a prerequisite for many cache-based attacks. Look for 'path mapping' issues where the server ignores parts of the URL (like extensions or extra slashes) while the cache uses those parts to decide what to store. A key signal is seeing a 'HIT' in the cache headers for a URL you just modified with a random extension. Avoid the mistake of assuming a bug is unexploitable just because it requires a specific header; sometimes those headers can be forced through other vulnerabilities like CORS or CSRF.
lesson.fix:
To fix this, the application should be configured to return a 404 Not Found error if a URL contains an unexpected file extension. Additionally, the server should send a 'Cache-Control: no-store, private' header for all responses containing sensitive data, which explicitly tells caches not to save the information. Finally, sensitive GraphQL operations should be restricted to POST requests only. Example header fix: 
Header set Cache-Control 'no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private'

title: How I Found an Unauthenticated GraphQL API Leaking User Data
summary_en: An unauthenticated GraphQL endpoint allowed anyone to query the entire user database, including PII, by exploiting missing authorization checks at the resolver level.

lesson.cause: The root cause was a failure to implement authorization at the resolver level (the specific code functions that fetch data for fields). While the server might have checked for a login at the main entry point, it failed to check if the user was allowed to access the specific 'users' data field. This allowed any visitor to send a POST request (a type of message used to send data to a server) to the /graphql endpoint and receive sensitive records without providing any credentials.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher identified a potential GraphQL endpoint, which is a specific web address (URL) where an API (a system for computers to talk to each other) can be reached.
2. They confirmed the endpoint was active by sending a minimal 'ping' query.
POST /graphql HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
{"query":"{__typename}"}
Why: The __typename field asks the server what kind of object it is; if it answers, it confirms GraphQL is running (a beginner gloss: it's like knocking on a door to see if anyone is home).
DISCOVERY
3. The researcher checked for 'Introspection,' a feature that lets you ask the server for a map of its entire database structure.
4. They sent a specialized query to download the full schema (the blueprint of all data types).
{"query":"query{__schema{types{name kind fields{name args{name} type{name kind ofType{name}}}}}}"}
Why: This returns every possible query, mutation (a command to change data), and field available on the server.
5. If introspection was blocked, the researcher would have used 'field suggestions' (where the server says 'Did you mean email?' when you guess wrong) to rebuild the map.
6. They also looked at client-side artifacts (the code sent to your browser) to find hidden query names.
EXPLOITATION
7. With the map in hand, the researcher looked for sensitive fields like 'users' or 'email'.
8. They prepared a request to fetch user data but intentionally removed all authentication headers (extra info like cookies or tokens that prove who you are).
9. They sent the unauthenticated request to the server.
POST /graphql HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
{"query":"{ users { id username name createdAt } }"}
Why: This asks for the ID, username, full name, and join date for all users. Because no login was provided, the server should have said 'Access Denied'.
10. The server incorrectly returned the data, proving that the 'resolver' ( the function that gets the data) had no security check.
11. The researcher then tested for BOLA (Broken Object-Level Authorization), which is when you can see other people's private data by guessing their ID number.
{"query":"{ user(id: 1337) { id email role } }"}
Why: This checks if a user can see the private email of user #1337.
IMPACT
12. To prove the bug could leak the entire database, the researcher used 'pagination' (breaking a long list into pages).
13. They used a 'cursor' (a digital bookmark) to ask for the next 100 users.
{"query":"{ users(first: 100, after: \"<cursor>\") { edges { node { id email } } pageInfo { endCursor hasNextPage } } }"}
Why: By following the 'endCursor' (the bookmark for the last item seen), an attacker can systematically download every single user record.
14. The researcher checked for 'Mutations' (commands that change data) to see if they could also delete or modify users without a login.
15. They checked for 'Query Batching,' which allows sending many requests at once to bypass speed limits.
16. Finally, they documented the findings, showing that anyone on the internet could steal the entire user list.
lesson.example: Imagine a library website at target.example. The website has a GraphQL API. The developer wrote a function (a resolver) to get book details, which is public. They also wrote a function to get 'MemberDetails' (names and home addresses). They forgot to add a 'checkLogin' step to the MemberDetails function. An attacker sends this request: POST /graphql {"query": "{ allMembers { fullName homeAddress } }"}. Even though the attacker isn't logged in, the server sees the request for 'allMembers', runs the unprotected function, and sends back the private addresses of every library member. This happens because the server was told HOW to get the data, but not WHO is allowed to see it.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs, always look for GraphQL endpoints like /graphql, /v1/graphql, or /api/graphql. Use introspection to map the attack surface, but don't give up if it's disabled; use tools to guess field names based on error messages. The most common mistake developers make is securing the 'front door' (the URL) but leaving the 'room doors' (the resolvers) unlocked. Always test sensitive queries with zero authentication to see if the server leaks data by default. A key variant is BOLA, where you are logged in but can access other users' data by changing an ID parameter.

title: HTTP Request Smuggling (TE.CL) to Session Hijacking via GraphQL
summary_en: An HTTP Request Smuggling vulnerability allowed an attacker to poison a back-end connection and capture a victim's full request. By redirecting this data into a GraphQL mutation, the attacker stored the victim's session cookies in their own support chat history.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by a TE.CL desynchronization (a state where two servers disagree on where a request ends) between a front-end proxy and a back-end server. The front-end prioritized the Transfer-Encoding header (a header telling the server data is sent in pieces), while the back-end prioritized the Content-Length header (a header telling the server the exact size of the data). This mismatch allowed the researcher to leave a 'partial' request hanging on the back-end connection. Furthermore, the /graphql endpoint (a specific web address for data queries) accepted form-encoded data, which is less strict than JSON, allowing the next user's request to be appended to a text parameter without crashing the application.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: The researcher identified the target's infrastructure, noting a front-end proxy (a middleman server) and a back-end application server.
Step 2: They tested for Request Smuggling (a technique to interfere with how a website processes sequences of HTTP requests).
DISCOVERY
Step 3: The researcher confirmed a TE.CL mismatch where the front-end used Transfer-Encoding and the back-end used Content-Length.
Step 4: They attempted to smuggle a request to a standard JSON API endpoint.
Step 5: They observed that the JSON parser (a tool that reads data in a specific structured format) failed because the victim's request broke the JSON structure.
Step 6: They searched for alternative endpoints and found /graphql, which accepted application/x-www-form-urlencoded data (a format where data is sent as key-value pairs like name=value).
EXPLOITATION
Step 7: The researcher crafted a 'trigger' request to desynchronize the connection.
POST /api/stich_transitionState?localeCode=en-US HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example.com
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Content-Length: [Calculated Length]

0
Why: The front-end sees the '0' and thinks the request is finished, but the back-end is told by Content-Length to keep waiting for more data.
Step 8: They appended a second, 'smuggled' request immediately after the trigger.
POST /graphql HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Why: This smuggled request (a hidden request tucked inside another) is what the back-end will process next.
Step 9: They used a GraphQL mutation (a type of request used to change or save data) that updates a support message.
operationName=updateMobileContact_deprecated&variables[request][message][text]=HIJACKED_REQUEST_BEGINS:
Why: This parameter (a piece of data sent to the server) will act as a container for the victim's data.
Step 10: They set a very large Content-Length for the smuggled GraphQL request.
Content-Length: [SMUGGLED_BODY_LENGTH + VICTIM_REQUEST_LENGTH]
Why: This makes the back-end 'hungry,' meaning it stays open and waits to swallow the next request that arrives on the connection.
Step 11: The researcher sent the combined payload (the actual malicious data being sent) to the server.
Step 12: A victim user sent a legitimate request to the server on the same connection.
GET /path/inbox HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example.com
Cookie: session_cookie=VICTIM_SESSION_VALUE
Why: Because the back-end was still 'hungry' from Step 10, it treated the victim's request as the continuation of the attacker's message text.
IMPACT
Step 13: The application processed the mutation, saving the attacker's message.
Step 14: The saved message now contained the victim's full request, including their Cookie (a small ID tag used to identify a logged-in user).
Step 15: The researcher logged into their own account and opened the support conversation.
Step 16: They viewed the message and successfully extracted the victim's session cookie.
Step 17: Using the stolen cookie, the researcher performed session hijacking (taking over another user's active session) to access the victim's account.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional site target.example.com that has a 'Update Profile Bio' feature. The server is vulnerable to TE.CL smuggling. An attacker sends a request to update their bio, but sets the Content-Length to be 500 bytes larger than the actual bio text. The request ends with 'bio=My bio is: '. When a victim user visits the site and their browser sends a request like 'GET /dashboard HTTP/1.1' followed by their private 'Cookie: session=12345', the server thinks this text is part of the attacker's bio. The attacker then simply views their own profile, and their bio now displays the victim's full request and session cookie.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for request smuggling, always look for endpoints that store user-supplied text, such as chat systems, profile bios, or support tickets. These are perfect 'sinks' for capturing smuggled data. If a JSON endpoint fails because the smuggled data is not valid JSON, look for form-encoded or GraphQL alternatives which are often more flexible. Use tools like Burp Suite's HTTP Request Smuggler to automate the detection of TE.CL and CL.TE mismatches. A common mistake is assuming a '400 Bad Request' means the site is not vulnerable; it often just means your payload needs adjustment to be syntactically valid for the application layer.
lesson.fix: To fix this, the organization should ensure that the front-end proxy and the back-end server use the same HTTP parsing library or configuration to avoid desynchronization. The most effective solution is to use HTTP/2 for the entire connection chain, as it uses a binary framing mechanism that eliminates the ambiguity of request boundaries. Additionally, the back-end should be configured to reject any request that contains both a Content-Length and a Transfer-Encoding header. Example fix in a configuration: 'http_protocol_options { strict_header_validation: true; }' or ensuring the proxy normalizes requests before forwarding them.

excerpt: A request parser disagreement between a front-end proxy and a back-end server can look like a simple `400 Bad Request` or connection desynchronization issue. The real security impact appears when that desynchronization can be turned into a reliable cross-request interaction. During an authorized assessment of web application, I found a TE.CL HTTP Request Smuggling condition. The front-end processed the request using: httpTransfer-Encoding: chunked while the back-end interpreted the request boundary using: httpContent-Length That mismatch allowed a crafted request to desynchronize the back-end

title: Exposure of Shareable AWS S3 Pre-Signed Download URLs for Paid Digital Products
summary_en: A GraphQL API endpoint leaked AWS S3 pre-signed URLs for paid digital products, allowing anyone to download restricted content without payment or authentication for up to 24 hours.

lesson.cause: The application's GraphQL API was designed to return a pre-signed S3 download URL in the 'listing.url' field by default when retrieving product information. The root cause was a failure to verify if the requesting user had actually purchased the product before generating this temporary access link. Because the URL functioned as a 'bearer token' (possession equals access), the application relied on the secrecy of the URL rather than proper authorization logic. Additionally, the URL expiration was set to a very long duration (86400 seconds), increasing the window for unauthorized access.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECONNAISSANCE
1. The researcher accessed the Linktree platform and navigated to the digital products section where creators sell files.
2. They used a proxy tool to intercept the HTTP requests (messages sent by your computer to a server asking for data) between the browser and the server.

DISCOVERY
3. The researcher identified a GraphQL request (a specific way for apps to ask for exactly the data they need) used to fetch product details.
4. They inspected the response from the server and found a field named 'listing.url'.
listing.url
Why: This field contained a long web address pointing directly to Amazon's storage service (AWS S3).
5. The researcher analyzed the URL and found several AWS signing parameters (special codes that grant temporary permission to a file).
?X-Amz-Algorithm=...&X-Amz-Credential=...&X-Amz-Date=...&X-Amz-Expires=86400&X-Amz-Signature=...
Why: These parameters prove to Amazon that the person who generated the link has permission to share the file. The 'X-Amz-Expires=86400' part means the link stays active for 86,400 seconds (24 hours).

EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher copied the entire URL from the GraphQL response.
7. They opened a new 'Incognito' or private browser window where they were NOT logged into Linktree.
8. They pasted the URL directly into the address bar and pressed Enter.
https://[bucket-name].s3.amazonaws.com/[file-path]?X-Amz-Algorithm=...[rest of signature]
Why: This tests if the link is a 'bearer credential' (a key that works for anyone who holds it, regardless of their identity).

IMPACT
9. The browser immediately began downloading the digital product (e.g., a PDF or image) that was supposed to be behind a paywall.
10. The researcher confirmed that no Linktree session or cookie (a small file used to remember your login status) was required to access the file.
11. This proved that any user—even one who hadn't paid—could obtain and share these links to bypass the store's payment system.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs, always inspect API responses (especially GraphQL and JSON) for long URLs containing 'Amz-Signature' or 'Signature'. These are often pre-signed URLs. Always test if these URLs can be opened in a private browser window without being logged in. If the URL points to content that should be paid or private, you have found a vulnerability. A common mistake is assuming that because a URL is long and 'random-looking,' it is secure; in reality, if the API gives it to an unauthorized user, the security is broken. Look for 'Expires' values—longer durations (like 24 hours) significantly increase the severity of the leak.
lesson.fix:
The application must separate 'viewing product info' from 'downloading the product.' The GraphQL query for product details should not include the download URL. Instead, the URL should only be generated through a specific 'Download' endpoint that first checks the database to ensure the current user has a valid purchase record for that specific item. Additionally, the 'X-Amz-Expires' value should be set to a very short time (e.g., 60 to 300 seconds) to minimize the risk of link sharing.

Fixed Logic:
1. User requests product info -> Server returns name and price (NO URL).
2. User clicks 'Download' -> Server checks: 'Has this user paid?'
3. If yes -> Server generates a 5-minute pre-signed URL and sends it.
4. If no -> Server returns '403 Forbidden'.

excerpt: While testing Linktree’s digital-product functionality, I identified an issue where GraphQL responses exposed AWS S3 pre-signed download URLs associated with digital products. The URLs were returned as part of the product/listing data and contained AWS S3 signing parameters. ## Discovery During testing of the digital-product functionality, I inspected the GraphQL responses returned when retrieving product information. A field similar to: `listing.url` contained an AWS S3 pre-signed URL. The URL included AWS signing parameters such as: * `X-Amz-Algorithm` * `X-Amz-Credential` * `X-Amz-Date` * `

title: Broken Function Level Authorization in Linktree GraphQL API Allows Lower-Privileged Admins to…
summary_en: A lower‑privileged Admin could call an Owner‑only GraphQL mutation and add new administrators, bypassing role‑based access control. The backend only checked authentication, not the user’s role, leading to privilege escalation.

lesson.cause: The GraphQL mutation that invites a new administrator lacked a function‑level authorization check. The server verified that the request came from an authenticated user but never confirmed that the user’s role was Owner. Because the resolver did not inspect the caller’s permissions, any authenticated Admin could invoke the mutation. This missing role verification is the root cause of the Broken Function Level Authorization vulnerability.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Capture a legitimate Owner request.
- Action: Log in as the Owner and use the browser’s developer tools to record the GraphQL request that adds an admin.
- Code: mutation { <owner_admin_invitation_mutation>( identifier: "<target-user>" accountId: "<account-id>" ) { ... } }
- Why: The HTTP request contains a GraphQL mutation (a structured operation sent over HTTP) that the Owner is allowed to execute.

Step 2: Identify the authentication cookie.
- Action: In the same network tab, note the "Cookie" header that carries the Owner’s session token.
- Why: A cookie is a small piece of data the browser sends with each request to prove the user is logged in.

EXPLOITATION
Step 3: Obtain an Admin session cookie.
- Action: Log out the Owner, log in as a lower‑privileged Admin, and copy the new "Cookie" header value.
- Why: This cookie represents an authenticated Admin user.

Step 4: Replace the Owner cookie with the Admin cookie.
- Action: In a tool like Burp Suite or curl, set the "Cookie" header to the Admin’s value while keeping the original request body unchanged.
- Why: The server will see a valid authenticated session but from a different role.

Step 5: Send the mutated request.
- Action: POST the same GraphQL payload (the mutation from Step 1) to the GraphQL endpoint using the Admin cookie.
- Code: POST /graphql HTTP/1.1\nHost: linktr.ee\nCookie: admin_session=...\nContent-Type: application/json\n\n{"query":"mutation { <owner_admin_invitation_mutation>(identifier:\"target@example.com\",accountId:\"12345\") { ... } }"}
- Why: The backend receives a valid mutation from an authenticated Admin; because it does not check the role, it processes the request.

Step 6: Observe the successful response.
- Action: The response contains a message like "<target-user> has been added as an admin".
- Why: The lack of role verification allowed the Admin to perform an Owner‑only operation.

IMPACT
Step 7: Verify the new admin exists.
- Action: Use the UI or another GraphQL query to list administrators and confirm the target user appears.
- Why: Confirms that privilege escalation succeeded.

STEP 8: Consider further abuse.
- Action: Repeat the process to add additional accounts or perform other Owner‑level mutations.
- Why: Once an attacker can create admins, they can maintain persistence and expand control.
lesson.takeaway: When testing GraphQL APIs, always enumerate every mutation and replay privileged ones with lower‑privileged accounts. Look for missing role checks in resolvers – the server may only verify authentication. Tools like Burp Suite, GraphQL Playground, or curl help capture and replay requests. Variants of this bug appear in REST endpoints that expose admin actions without proper RBAC, or in RPC services that skip permission checks. Beginners often forget to swap the authentication token and keep the original request body unchanged, which leads to false‑negative results.

title: The Butterfly Effect: Turning Overlooked Misconfigurations into Zero Click Account Takeover
summary_en: A chain of overlooked GraphQL misconfigurations — enabled suggestions, an IDOR that enumerated students and admins, and a login mutation that accepted an empty password when loggedSSO=true — escalated into zero-click takeover of any account on an e-learning platform.
summary_ar: سلسلة من سوء الإعدادات في GraphQL — تفعيل الـ suggestions، وثغرة IDOR لسرد الطلاب والمشرفين، وmutation تسجيل دخول تقبل كلمة مرور فارغة عند تمرير loggedSSO=true — تحوّلت إلى استيلاء كامل (zero-click) على أي حساب في منصة تعليم إلكتروني.

lesson.cause_ar: السبب الجذري ليس ثغرة واحدة بل سلسلة إعدادات خاطئة تراكمت فوق بعضها. أولاً، خاصية GraphQL suggestions كانت مفعّلة في بيئة الإنتاج، فسرّبت أسماء الـ queries والـ mutations المتاحة للمهاجم. ثانيًا، الـ resolvers الخاصة بـ student(id) و administrator(id) كانت ترجع بيانات أي كائن بمجرد تمرير الـ id من غير أي تحقق أن المستخدم الحالي يملك صلاحية الوصول لهذا الكائن — غياب تام للـ object-level authorization. ثالثًا — والأخطر — الـ backend الخاص بـ loginStudent لم يفرض فعليًا القيد non-nullable على حقل password رغم أن الـ schema يعرّفه بعلامة !، وكان تمرير loggedSSO=true يختصر التحقق من كلمة المرور بالكامل. وأخيرًا، توكن المشرف كان يتطلب claim إضافي اسمه adminLevel داخل الـ JWT، وهذا الـ claim كان متاحًا عبر ثغرة الـ IDOR. كل عنصر لوحده يبدو منخفض الخطورة، لكنه معًا شكّل سلسلة استيلاء كامل على الحسابات.
lesson.walkthrough_ar:
الخطوة 1: السياق — الباحث كان في اختبار اختراق لمنصة تعليم إلكتروني للطلاب (تطوير داخلي) أثناء ترحيلها من مزوّد استضافة خارجي إلى بيئة سحابية جديدة، والهدف foo.target.com. ليه: التطبيقات المطوّرة داخليًا غالبًا مليانة إعدادات مهملة، والترحيل فرصة ذهبية لظهور أخطاء.
الخطوة 2: أثناء رسم خريطة التطبيق اكتشف أن الـ API مبني على GraphQL. ليه: GraphQL يسمح بطلب بيانات محددة بدقة، وسوء إعداده يفتح أبوابًا كثيرة.
الخطوة 3: لاحظ أن خاصية GraphQL suggestions مفعّلة في الإنتاج، فبدأت تقترح عليه الـ queries والـ mutations المتاحة. ليه: تسريب بنية الـ schema يساعد المهاجم في صياغة هجمات أدق.
الخطوة 4: اكتشف IDOR في query باسم student — بجلسة طالب عادية استطاع سرد بيانات أي طالب عبر تغيير الـ id. الطلب:
POST /graphql
Host: foo.target.com
Authorization: Bearer [Student JWT]
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "operationName": "student",
  "variables": {},
  "query": "query student {\n  student(id:1234) {\n    firstName\n    lastName\n    profile\n    affiliation\n    email\n    createdAt\n    __typename\n  }\n}"
}
الاستجابة رجعت بيانات Alan Turing كاملة (email و affiliation و profile). ليه: الـ resolver بيرجع بيانات أي id من غير ما يتحقق إن الطالب صاحب الجلسة هو نفسه صاحب الـ id.
الخطوة 5: نفس الفكرة مع administrator(id:500) — سرد بيانات المشرفين ومنها adminLevel و trainerId. الاستجابة رجعت بيانات Linus Torvalds مع adminLevel: 2. ليه: نفس غياب الـ authorization على مستوى الـ object.
الخطوة 6: حلّل ملفات JavaScript الخاصة بالتطبيق ووجد mutation باسم loginStudent فيها email و password و loggedSSO وكلها معلمة بعلامة ! (non-nullable). ليه: ملفات الـ JS بتسرّب بنية الـ API الداخلية.
الخطوة 7: جرّب تمرير loggedSSO: true مع إيميل طالب وبدون تعيين كلمة المرور — فوجئ بأن السيرفر أعاد access token للطالب. ليه: الـ backend ما فرضش الـ non-null رغم تعريف الـ schema، وflag الـ loggedSSO اختصر التحقق من كلمة المرور.
الخطوة 8: الطلب النهائي للاستيلاء على حساب طالب:
POST /graphql
Host: foo.target.tld
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "operationName": "LoginStudent",
  "variables": {
    "email": "alan.turing@student.tld",
    "password": "",
    "loggedSSO": true
  },
  "query": "mutation LoginStudent($email: String, $uid: String, $password: String, $loggedSSO: Boolean!, $dataToUpdate: String) {\n  loginStudent(\n    email: $email\n    uid: $uid\n    password: $password\n    loggedSSO: $loggedSSO\n    dataToUpdate: $dataToUpdate\n  )\n}"
}
الاستجابة رجعت JWT يخص الطالب. ليه: كلمة المرور الفارغة مرّت لأن التحقق الفعلي مشغّل على الـ loggedSSO مش على الـ password.
الخطوة 9: بدمج الـ IDOR مع الـ bypass بقدر ياخد أي حساب طالب بإيميله فقط. ليه: الـ IDOR وفّر قائمة الإيميلات والـ bypass وفّر الدخول.
الخطوة 10: جرّب نفس الأسلوب بإيميل مشرف — حصل على session token لكنه ما قدرش يستخدم مزايا المشرف. ليه: توكن المشرف لازم يحوي claim إضافي اسمه adminLevel داخل جسم الـ JWT.
الخطوة 11: عرف من نتيجة الـ IDOR إن الـ adminLevel بيرجع مع بيانات المشرف (مثلاً adminLevel: 2). ليه: الـ claim ده هو اللي بيميّز صلاحيات المشرف.
الخطوة 12: حاول فرض adminLevel في الطلب لكن بدون نجاح. ليه: السيرفر مش بيقبل claim مفروض من العميل.
الخطوة 13: جرّب تغيير الـ mutation إلى LoginAdmin — فظهرت رسالة خطأ من GraphQL suggestions: Cannot query field "LoginAdmin" on type "Mutation". Did you mean "loginAdmin" or "signupAdmin"? ليه: الـ suggestions كشفت الاسم الصحيح للـ mutation.
الخطوة 14: استخدم loginAdmin بنفس منطق loggedSSO=true وبدون كلمة مرور — نجح bypass لصلاحيات المشرف. ليه: نفس الخلل في التحقق من كلمة المرور موجود في mutation تسجيل دخول المشرف، فاكتملت السلسلة من IDOR إلى استيلاء كامل على حساب مشرف.
lesson.takeaway_ar: أول ما تشوف GraphQL في هدف، جرّب فورًا الـ introspection والـ suggestions — لو رجّعوا أسماء عمليات، دي إشارة قوية إن الـ schema مسرّب. دوّر في ملفات الـ JS على أسماء mutations خاصة بالدخول، وابحث عن أي parameter من نوع flag (زي loggedSSO أو isSSO أو rememberMe) ممكن يختصر التحقق. قارن دايماً بين تعريف الـ schema (علامة !) والسلوك الفعلي للـ backend — التناقض بينهم كنز حقيقي. ولو لقيت IDOR في query بيرجّع بيانات مستخدمين، استخدمه لبناء قائمة أهداف ثم ادمجه مع أي bypass للدخول. الفكرة الكبرى: ثغرة low severity مش نهاية القصة، جرّب تركّبها مع غيرها.
